title: Reading a Contract, Policy, or Terms of Service
goal: Read a lease and an app's terms of service closely enough to state what you're actually agreeing to, what conditions apply, and what's buried in the fine print.

prompts: From memory: state the three lateral-reading questions (Session 8).

vocab.def: something you are required to do under the agreement (pay rent by the 1st; give 30 days' notice)

one specific section or provision of a contract, usually addressing one issue. Contracts are read clause by clause, not as one flowing paragraph — a single clause can override the general impression given elsewhere in the document
to voluntarily give up a right you would otherwise have
examples: By signing, you waive your right to a jury trial and agree to arbitration instead

facts: surveys of internet users consistently find almost no one reads a terms-of-service document in full before clicking "agree" — the length and legal language are part of the design, not an accident.
a contract's friendliest-sounding sentence and its most restrictive clause can both be true at once — reading only the friendly parts is exactly how the restrictive parts go unnoticed.
prime.question: name one real contract, lease, or terms-of-service agreement you've clicked "agree" to or signed without reading in full.
prime.intro: Two facts before you read: (1) surveys of internet users consistently find almost no one reads a terms-of-service document in full before clicking "agree" — the length and legal language are part of the design, not an accident. (2) a contract's friendliest-sounding sentence and its most restrictive clause can both be true at once — reading only the friendly parts is exactly how the restrictive parts go unnoticed. Orienting question: name one real contract, lease, or terms-of-service agreement you've clicked "agree" to or signed without reading in full.

write.task: Write a paragraph (6–8 sentences): pick the lease OR the app terms, and explain, as if to a friend about to sign, the two things they most need to know that aren't obvious from a casual read. Use obligation, clause, and waive correctly at least once each.

items.q: Compare your answers with the model answer.
items.a: late — the clause explicitly says "regardless of postmark date," so the mailing date is irrelevant, only receipt/processing counts. Q3: notice alone is not enough — all three of notice + fee + successful re-renting must occur; rent obligation continues until then. Q6: no — anonymized/aggregated data can be kept "indefinitely" even after deletion, so "deletion" does not mean complete erasure.

items.q: Could you answer Q1, Q3, and Q6 correctly without rereading the source text? These three are the ones most people get wrong on a first, casual read.

passages.title: A lease excerpt
paragraphs: §2. Term. This lease begins June 1 and ends May 31 of the following year (the "Term"). Tenant may not terminate this lease early except as provided in §7.

§4. Rent and Late Fees. Rent is due on the 1st of each month. A payment is considered late if received after 5:00 PM on the 3rd of the month, regardless of postmark date or date sent. A late fee of $75 plus $10 per additional day applies to any late payment. Two late payments within any six-month period constitute a material breach of this lease.

§6. Security Deposit. Tenant's security deposit of one month's rent will be returned within 30 days of move-out, less deductions for damage beyond normal wear and tear, unpaid rent, or cleaning fees. "Normal wear and tear" does not include, and will result in deductions for: carpet stains of any kind, nail holes larger than a standard picture hook, or any repainting required to restore walls to their original color.

§7. Early Termination. Tenant may terminate this lease before the end of the Term only by (a) providing 60 days' written notice, AND (b) paying an early termination fee equal to two months' rent, AND (c) the unit being successfully re-rented to a new tenant approved by Landlord — until all three conditions are met, Tenant remains responsible for rent.

§11. Dispute Resolution. Any dispute arising under this lease shall be resolved through binding arbitration rather than in court, and Tenant waives the right to a jury trial or to participate in a class action related to this lease.

questions.q: If rent is due on the 1st, and a tenant mails a check on the 1st that arrives and is processed on the 4th, is that payment late under §4? Quote the exact phrase that answers this.

A tenant assumes "normal wear and tear" covers minor scuffed paint after a year of living there. Does §6 actually agree? Quote the clause and explain the gap between the tenant's assumption and the actual text.

A tenant wants to move out 90 days early because of a new job in another city. List, in order, every condition from §7 that must ALL be true before the lease is actually terminated — is giving 60 days' notice, by itself, enough?
What right does §11 make the tenant waive? Why might someone sign this without realizing they gave up that specific right — what makes this kind of clause easy to skim past?

passages.title: A phone app's terms of service excerpt
paragraphs: Excerpt — MoodTrack App Terms of Service

By creating an account, you grant MoodTrack a worldwide, royalty-free, perpetual license to use, reproduce, and create derivative works from any content you submit, including journal entries and mood data, for the purposes of operating, improving, and marketing the Service, including use of anonymized or aggregated data by third-party partners. You may request account deletion at any time; deletion removes your account from active use but anonymized or aggregated data derived from your content prior to deletion may be retained indefinitely.

questions.q: In plain language, what is the user actually agreeing to let the company do with their private journal entries?
The passage says you can "request account deletion at any time" — does that mean all your data is deleted? Quote the exact phrase that limits this.

moves.title: reading a legal document
paragraphs: A careful reader of a contract does not read it once, top to bottom, and trust the overall impression. They read for: (1) what am I obligated to do, and by when; (2) what conditions trigger extra fees, penalties, or a loss of a right; (3) what rights am I giving up (waiving) that I might not notice I'm giving up; (4) does a specific clause later in the document quietly narrow or contradict a friendlier-sounding sentence earlier.

roles.prompt: Which single clause, across both documents, would surprise most people who signed without reading closely?
What question would you ask a landlord or a company directly before signing, based on what you found?
Explain "waive" using the arbitration clause as the example.
In two sentences, state the biggest gap between what each document sounds like at a glance and what it actually says.
